Recent work supports separating stable preferences from changing intent. [Teddy (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ipm.2023.103619) adaptively partitions history into dominant trends and scattered interests, using temporal convolutions and pooled MLP features respectively. [IDCLRec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.07096) extracts consistent interests through causal cross-attention, models residual behavior as dynamic intent, and adds item-aware contrastive supervision. Its criticism of arbitrary fixed intent counts is relevant: multiple representation heads alone do not establish meaningful disentanglement.

Temporal modeling offers a complementary axis. [HyperHawkes](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=t0q7KbmB7o) combines clustered latent intents, temporal processes for recurring consumption, and attention mixtures for immediate interests. [DSRec (September 2026 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21548) separates historical preferences from local intent, using distinct state-space encoders and inter-click intervals to modulate the short-term branch. These approaches motivate distinguishing sequence position, elapsed time, and intent recurrence rather than assuming uniform recency decay; their reported benchmark improvements do not establish gains under this task’s evaluator.

Practical inference for the constrained SASRec search: retain the sequence encoder, add a pooled historical-interest branch and a recent-window branch, then learn a gate conditioned on observed history and timestamp gaps. A few latent interest queries could preserve alternative purposes, with a modest diversity penalty tested against representation collapse. Purchase saturation remains a hypothesis requiring validation: recurring interest supports renewed demand, while recent consumption may suppress it. Because recommendations exclude seen items, test such effects across related unseen items; do not infer conformity, satisfaction, or simulator traits from interaction histories.
